title: The model of rules, and what it leaves out
subtitle: Dworkin's attack on Hart: rules, principles and policies
objectives: State Dworkin's distinction between rules, principles and policies, and explain why he thinks Hart's 'model of rules' cannot account for principles
Explain how Riggs v Palmer illustrates a principle operating as binding law without any pedigree in a rule of recognition
Identify how a Hartian positivist might respond to Dworkin's critique, and why the debate remains unresolved

leadingAuthorities.citation: Dworkin, Taking Rights Seriously (1977), esp. 'The Model of Rules I'
leadingAuthorities.role: Sets out the rules/principles/policies distinction and the attack on Hart's rule of recognition as a pedigree test for law
Dworkin's central illustration of a legal principle operating as binding law despite having no source in any enacted rule

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students often summarise this debate as 'Dworkin proved Hart wrong', which flattens a genuinely live argument into a settled score. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of understanding, this brief note appears: 'You can state Dworkin's distinction — this lesson checks whether you can also state the strongest Hartian reply, and explain exactly what's still contested.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool leans on scenarios: whether a given standard is behaving like a rule or a principle, and how each side of the debate would classify it.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and make sure you can restate Hart's model of rules accurately before reading Dworkin's attack on it — you need the target in view before you can judge whether the attack lands.

overview.hook: A New York court in 1889 faced a will that was, on its face, perfectly valid — properly signed, witnessed, and naming the murderer as sole heir. The murderer had killed the testator specifically to collect. Nothing in the statute of wills said a beneficiary forfeits an inheritance for killing the person who left it to them. The court denied him the money anyway. Ronald Dworkin thought that single case broke a theory H.L.A. Hart had spent a career building — and the argument he built on it is still argued over today.
overview.lawStatedNotice: This lesson presents an unresolved theoretical debate as contested scholarship, not settled doctrine — Hartian positivists have replies to every move described here, and neither side has conceded.

parts.heading: The target: Hart's model of rules
parts.voice: expository — restates the target precisely before the attack begins
body: To understand Dworkin's critique you first need Hart's theory, from Lesson 5, restated with precision. Hart's positivism holds that a legal system is, at root, a union of primary rules (rules of conduct) and secondary rules (rules about rules) — chief among them the rule of recognition, the master social rule officials use to identify which other rules count as valid law.

On this picture, whether a standard is law is a question of pedigree: does it trace back, through a chain of validity, to the rule of recognition's criteria — enactment by Parliament, decision by a court of record, and so on? Content and moral merit are irrelevant to that test; only source matters. Dworkin calls this the 'model of rules', and it is exactly this pedigree test he sets out to break.

Dworkin's challenge, stated plainly, is this: legal reasoning is full of standards that judges treat as binding, that decide real cases, and that cannot be traced to any rule of recognition's pedigree test at all. If that's true, Hart's model has left something essential out of the picture of what law actually is.

components.definition: Dworkin's label for Hart's positivism: the claim that a legal system consists of rules identified by their pedigree — their source, traced through a rule of recognition — with no role for standards whose authority rests on their content or moral weight.

interaction.prompt: On Hart's model of rules, does a standard count as law because of where it comes from (its pedigree) or because of how morally compelling its content is?
options: Its pedigree — the source it can be traced to via the rule of recognition
Its content — how morally compelling the standard is
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Hart's positivism is a pedigree test: a rule counts as law because it was made in the right way by the right body, not because of anything about its moral content.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at what the rule of recognition actually tests for — it's a source-based test (pedigree), not a content-based or moral test. That's exactly the feature Dworkin's attack targets.

parts.heading: Rules, principles, policies: three different kinds of standard
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Dworkin distinguishes three kinds of legal standard, and the distinction between the first two is the engine of his whole argument.

A rule applies in an all-or-nothing fashion: if the rule's stated conditions are satisfied, it dictates a result, full stop — subject only to exceptions that, in principle, could all be listed. A speed limit either applies to your journey or it doesn't; there's no sense in which a speed limit can apply 'a bit'.

A principle is different in kind. It states a reason arguing in one direction, but it doesn't dictate a particular result and it doesn't need to be exhaustively listed with its exceptions. Principles have what Dworkin calls a dimension of weight: two principles can point in opposite directions in the same case, and a court must judge which weighs more here, without either principle being invalidated by losing that contest. 'No one shall profit from their own wrong' can be outweighed by a stronger principle in a different case — and it remains just as much a principle as before.

A policy, finally, is a standard that sets a goal to be reached — usually some improvement in economic, political or social welfare, such as reducing road accidents — rather than protecting an individual right. Dworkin's attack focuses on principles, not policies, because principles are the standards judges most often treat as binding rights-claims, not mere goals to be traded off.

components.label: Rules vs principles vs policies
points: Rules — apply all-or-nothing; if valid and applicable, they dictate the outcome
Principles — have a dimension of weight; can conflict without either being invalidated; the stronger wins in that case only
Policies — set a collective goal (e.g. economic welfare), rather than protecting an individual right
Dworkin's target is principles specifically: standards courts treat as binding on individual rights, yet which have no pedigree in a rule of recognition

interaction.prompt: Put these statements about a legal standard in the order that shows it behaving like a principle rather than a rule.
items: A court identifies a standard that favours one party
A competing standard favouring the other party is identified
The court weighs the two, finding one has greater force on these facts
The losing standard is applied with reduced or no effect here, but remains valid law for future cases
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the 'dimension of weight' in action: both standards remain valid; the case turns on which weighs more here, not on one being knocked out of the system.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the final step — a rule that loses a conflict is usually invalidated or amended; a principle that loses a conflict simply carries less weight on these particular facts and remains good law for the next case.

parts.heading: Riggs v Palmer: a principle without pedigree
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: Elmer Palmer murdered his grandfather, Francis Palmer, by poisoning him — precisely because Elmer knew he stood to inherit under his grandfather's will and feared the old man might change it. Convicted of the murder, Elmer nonetheless claimed the estate the will left him. Nothing in New York's statute of wills said a beneficiary forfeits an inheritance for killing the testator; the formalities of execution were all satisfied.

The New York Court of Appeals denied Elmer the inheritance anyway. It reasoned that 'no one shall be permitted to profit by his own fraud, or to take advantage of his own wrong' — a principle so deeply embedded in the law that it operates even where no statute states it, cutting across the literal words of the statute of wills to defeat a result the legislature plainly never intended to permit.

This is Dworkin's central exhibit. The 'no profit from wrong' principle was not enacted by any legislature and cannot be traced through any pedigree test to a rule of recognition — it isn't a statute, a precedent creating a binding ratio on these exact facts, or anything Hart's model of rules can locate. Yet the court treated it as binding law, sufficient to override the literal statute. If Dworkin is right that this really was law the court was applying — not something the judges made up on the spot — then Hart's model has missed something about what law actually contains.

components.factsShort: A grandson murdered his grandfather to inherit under the will before it could be changed; the will's formalities were entirely valid.
components.ratioShort: A beneficiary cannot profit from a will by murdering the testator, even though nothing in the statute of wills says so — the principle that no one may profit from their own wrong overrides the literal statutory text.

expanded.facts: Francis Palmer executed a will leaving most of his estate to his grandson Elmer, with smaller gifts to Elmer's mother and two daughters of the testator. Elmer, aware of the will and fearing his grandfather might revoke or alter it, poisoned him. Elmer was convicted of murder. He then sought to take under the will as executed.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The court held that all laws, as well as all contracts, 'may be controlled in their operation and effect by general, fundamental maxims of the common law. No one shall be permitted to profit by his own fraud, or to take advantage of his own wrong, or to found any claim upon his own iniquity, or to acquire property by his own crime.' The statute of wills was to be read as if this exception were implicit within it.
expanded.significance: Dworkin uses Riggs v Palmer as his central example of a principle functioning as binding law with no source traceable to a rule of recognition — the case is the pivot of his argument that positivism's pedigree test cannot capture everything judges treat as law.

interaction.prompt: In the extract from Riggs v Palmer below, highlight the sentence stating the principle the court applied.
interaction.passage: All laws, as well as all contracts, may be controlled in their operation and effect by general, fundamental maxims of the common law. No one shall be permitted to profit by his own fraud, or to take advantage of his own wrong, or to found any claim upon his own iniquity, or to acquire property by his own crime. These maxims are dictated by public policy, have their foundation in universal law administered in all civilised countries, and will, when applied to the construction of wills, defeat the intention of the testator only so far as it would work manifest injustice.
interaction.ratioSentence: No one shall be permitted to profit by his own fraud, or to take advantage of his own wrong, or to found any claim upon his own iniquity, or to acquire property by his own crime.

parts.heading: The threat to the rule of recognition, and the 'one right answer' thesis
parts.voice: argumentative — states Dworkin's strongest claim plainly
body: Dworkin's argument then runs as follows. Principles like the one in Riggs are treated by courts as binding — they decide real cases, overriding literal statutory text. But they have no pedigree: no rule of recognition test of enactment or precedent-ratio can explain why this particular maxim, among countless moral platitudes, counts as law rather than mere background morality. Their authority instead rests on something about their content — how well they fit and justify the rest of the legal system, and how much weight they carry as principles of political morality.

If that's right, Hart's central claim — that a master rule of recognition, tested only by pedigree, can identify everything that counts as law in a system — is false. Law, for Dworkin, includes principles identified partly by their moral and institutional fit, not solely by their source.

This sets up Dworkin's most contested claim, developed fully in Lesson 9: the 'one right answer' thesis. If judges deciding hard cases are applying binding principles — not merely exercising a discretion Hart's theory says arises whenever the rules run out — then even the hardest cases may have a single correct legal answer, discoverable through principled reasoning, rather than a gap the judge is legally free to fill however they see fit.

components.definition: Dworkin's claim that even genuinely hard cases have a single correct legal answer, because judges are bound by principles (not merely rules), and the right answer is the one that best fits and morally justifies the legal system as a whole. Examined in full, and critically assessed, in Lesson 9.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that Dworkin's argument depends on showing that Hart's rule of recognition could never, even in principle, be adjusted to include principles?
sliderLabels: Confident — Dworkin shows this is impossible in principle
Not confident — that's exactly what Hartians dispute, not something Dworkin has settled
interaction.correctPosition: Not confident — that's exactly what Hartians dispute, not something Dworkin has settled
interaction.explanation: This is precisely the live disagreement examined next. Dworkin argues the model of rules as Hart originally stated it cannot capture principles; whether a modified rule of recognition could is contested, not conceded.

parts.heading: The Hartian reply — and a debate that continues
parts.voice: even-handed — states the strongest response fairly, without declaring a winner
body: A committed Hartian positivist has a real answer here, and it's worth stating as strongly as Dworkin's attack. One line of reply — developed by positivists sometimes called 'soft' or 'inclusive' positivists — accepts that principles can be law, but denies this defeats Hart's model: the rule of recognition, they argue, is simply a social convention among officials, and there is no reason in principle why that convention could not itself include a criterion referring to moral principles or 'fit' with the rest of the system, alongside pedigree tests like enactment. On this reply, Riggs v Palmer doesn't refute the rule of recognition — it just shows the rule of recognition in a given system can be more complex than a simple checklist of sources.

A second Hartian line questions whether the 'no profit from wrong' maxim really was binding law before Riggs, or whether the New York court was doing something closer to what Hart called judicial discretion in the penumbra — reasonably extending the law to reach a just result in a hard case, rather than mechanically applying a pre-existing legal principle that was there all along waiting to be found.

Dworkin has responses to both of these moves in turn, which is exactly why this remains a genuine, unresolved dispute rather than a case either side has settled. What should not survive this lesson is the flattened version — 'Dworkin refuted Hart' — because Hartians have not conceded, and the argument runs on through decades of subsequent jurisprudence, including Hart's own posthumous reply in the postscript to The Concept of Law.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often write that Riggs v Palmer 'proves' positivism is wrong, as if the case settles the theoretical debate.
components.whyItsWrong: A single case can illustrate an argument; it cannot by itself refute a general jurisprudential theory. Inclusive positivists accept Riggs as consistent with a suitably adjusted rule of recognition, and the debate over whether that adjustment is available, or is itself a concession to Dworkin, remains live and contested.

interaction.prompt: Which statement best describes the current state of the Hart–Dworkin debate over principles, as this lesson presents it?
options: Dworkin's argument in 'The Model of Rules I' settled the question; positivism has no answer to Riggs v Palmer
Hartian positivists, especially 'inclusive' positivists, have developed replies that remain contested rather than defeated — the debate is genuinely unresolved
Hart abandoned legal positivism entirely after reading Dworkin's critique
interaction.trapExplanation: The first option overstates Dworkin's victory; the third invents a capitulation that never happened — Hart maintained and refined his positivism, including in the postscript to The Concept of Law. The accurate position is an ongoing, contested debate.

testPool.prompt: Name the three kinds of legal standard Dworkin distinguishes in 'The Model of Rules I'.
State the maxim the New York Court of Appeals invoked in Riggs v Palmer to deny Elmer Palmer his inheritance.
acceptableAnswers: no one shall profit from their own wrong
no one may profit by their own fraud or wrong
a person cannot profit from their own crime
testPool.modelAnswer: No one shall be permitted to profit by their own fraud, or to take advantage of their own wrong, or to acquire property by their own crime.

testPool.prompt: On Dworkin's account, are principles standards a judge may freely disregard, or standards a judge is bound to take into account when deciding a case?
options: Standards the judge may freely disregard
Standards the judge is bound to take into account, even though they can be outweighed

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that a principle, once outweighed in a particular case, is thereby invalidated as law in the way a repealed rule is?
sliderLabels: Confident — outweighed does not mean invalidated
testPool.explanation: A principle that loses a weighing contest in one case remains valid law and can prevail in a different case with different competing considerations — this is the 'dimension of weight' that distinguishes principles from all-or-nothing rules.

testPool.prompt: Put the events of Riggs v Palmer in chronological order.
items: Francis Palmer executes a will naming Elmer as principal beneficiary
Elmer poisons his grandfather, fearing the will might later be changed
The court denies Elmer his inheritance despite the will's formal validity

testPool.prompt: Which best states the difference between how a rule and a principle behave when they conflict with a competing standard in the same case?
options: A rule that loses is generally invalidated or amended; a principle that loses simply carries less weight here but remains good law
A rule that loses is reweighed for next time; a principle that loses is permanently struck from the legal system
There is no meaningful difference — Dworkin uses the terms interchangeably
testPool.trapExplanation: The second option reverses Dworkin's own distinction; the third denies that a distinction exists at all, which is precisely what Dworkin's argument depends on.

testPool.prompt: In this extract summarising Dworkin's argument, highlight the sentence identifying exactly what Hart's rule of recognition cannot explain.
testPool.passage: Riggs v Palmer shows a court treating a standard as binding law. That standard was never enacted by a legislature, and it does not derive from the ratio of a specific prior case on these facts. No pedigree test — no test of source alone — can explain why this maxim, among countless moral generalities, counts as law rather than background morality. Its authority instead rests on its fit with, and its weight within, the legal system as a whole.
testPool.ratioSentence: No pedigree test — no test of source alone — can explain why this maxim, among countless moral generalities, counts as law rather than background morality.

testPool.prompt: In the Riggs extract — 'these maxims are dictated by public policy, have their foundation in universal law administered in all civilised countries, and will... defeat the intention of the testator only so far as it would work manifest injustice' — which phrase most directly supports Dworkin's claim that the standard applied has no pedigree in an enacted rule?
options: 'have their foundation in universal law administered in all civilised countries'
testPool.explanation: Grounding the maxim in 'universal law' rather than any specific New York statute or precedent is exactly the absence of pedigree Dworkin relies on — the court is not citing a source that a rule of recognition's pedigree test could locate.

testPool.prompt: A tenancy statute states a landlord 'shall' return a deposit within 14 days of a tenancy ending, with no exceptions listed. A court is later asked to create an exception for a tenant who deliberately destroyed the property to trigger a deposit dispute. Applying Dworkin's rules/principles distinction, how should this statutory deposit provision itself be classified?
options: As a principle — it merely provides a reason in one direction, to be weighed against others
As a rule — it applies in all-or-nothing fashion once its stated conditions are met, subject only to exceptions that could in principle be listed
As a policy — it exists to promote the collective welfare of the rental market
testPool.explanation: A clear statutory 'shall... within 14 days' provision is a paradigm rule: it applies all-or-nothing once its conditions are satisfied. Any exception for bad-faith tenants would have to come from a separate principle (such as 'no profit from one's own wrong') operating alongside, not from redefining the rule itself as a principle.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that shows the standard being applied is functioning as a Dworkinian principle rather than an all-or-nothing rule.
testPool.scenarioText: A court considers two competing standards in a contract dispute: the strict rule that a signed document is binding regardless of its terms, and the standard that a party should not benefit from their own bad-faith concealment. The court holds that, on these particular facts, the concealment standard outweighs the strict-enforcement standard, while noting the strict rule remains fully valid law for ordinary cases.
tappableSpans: a signed document is binding regardless of its terms
should not benefit from their own bad-faith concealment
remains fully valid law for ordinary cases
testPool.feedbackCorrect: That's the dimension of weight in action — one standard prevails on these facts without the other being struck down, which is exactly how Dworkin says principles, not rules, behave.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the language of weighing rather than validity. The moment the court says one standard 'outweighs' another, while both remain valid, you're looking at principles being balanced, not a rule being applied or repealed.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that would most concern a Hartian positivist defending the rule of recognition against Dworkin's critique.
testPool.scenarioText: A court applies a standard that has never been enacted by any legislature, does not appear in the ratio of any binding precedent on these facts, and is justified only by reference to how well it fits the rest of the legal system's moral commitments — yet the court insists it was bound to apply it as law.
tappableSpans: never been enacted by any legislature
does not appear in the ratio of any binding precedent
justified only by reference to how well it fits the rest of the legal system's moral commitments
insists it was bound to apply it as law
testPool.correctSpan: justified only by reference to how well it fits the rest of the legal system's moral commitments
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right — a standard whose authority rests on moral fit rather than any traceable source is exactly what a pure pedigree test struggles to explain, which is the crux of Dworkin's challenge to the rule of recognition.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: The absence of a statute or precedent is necessary to Dworkin's point but not the sharpest version of it. What should worry a Hartian most is the source of the standard's authority being moral fit rather than any pedigree at all.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario best illustrates the Riggs v Palmer pattern Dworkin relies on — a binding standard with no pedigree overriding a literally satisfied rule?
testPool.scenarioA: A statute requires a written contract for the sale of land; a court refuses to enforce an oral agreement because the statutory formality was never met, exactly as the statute requires.
testPool.scenarioB: An insurance policy is, on its literal wording, payable on the policyholder's death by any cause; a court refuses payment where the beneficiary murdered the policyholder to claim it, applying the unwritten principle that no one may profit from their own crime.
testPool.explanation: B mirrors Riggs exactly: the literal instrument's terms are satisfied, but an unenacted principle with no pedigree overrides the literal result. A is a straightforward, all-or-nothing application of a rule as written — no principle is needed to explain the outcome.

testPool.prompt: A trustee negligently, but not fraudulently, mismanages a trust and this happens to increase their own beneficial share under its terms. There is no fraud, deceit or intentional wrongdoing — only carelessness. Applying the Riggs principle as Dworkin frames it, is a court compelled to reach the same result as in Riggs?
options: Yes — any gain connected to a breach of duty automatically triggers the principle
Not necessarily — the principle's weight depends on the wrongdoing involved, and mere negligence is a materially weaker case than deliberate murder to accelerate inheritance
No — principles never apply outside cases of inheritance
testPool.explanation: Because principles have a dimension of weight rather than operating all-or-nothing, how strongly 'no profit from wrong' applies depends on the facts — deliberate, serious wrongdoing (murder) weighs very differently from mere negligence, and a court would have to weigh this principle against countervailing considerations rather than apply it mechanically.

testPool.prompt: An employee is named as the sole beneficiary of her employer's staff pension scheme. She is later found to have caused the employer's insolvency through a sustained, deliberate fraud, and the pension scheme's rules say nothing about forfeiture for misconduct. Analyse, using Dworkin's rules/principles framework and Riggs v Palmer, whether a court could deny her the pension despite the scheme's literal rules entitling her to it — and note how a Hartian positivist might respond to that analysis.
factsToOrder: The employee is named sole beneficiary under the pension scheme's rules
She deliberately and fraudulently caused the employer's insolvency
The scheme's rules contain no forfeiture provision for misconduct
The literal wording of the scheme entitles her to the pension

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether a court could deny the employee her pension despite the scheme's literal rules, by applying a Riggs-style principle rather than the scheme's rule as written.
modelAnswer.rule: Dworkin argues that principles such as 'no one shall profit from their own wrong' are binding law even without pedigree in an enacted rule, and can override a literally satisfied rule where the beneficiary's own serious wrongdoing produced the entitlement claimed (Riggs v Palmer). A Hartian positivist would reply that any such result must ultimately be traceable to a rule of recognition that can accommodate moral or 'fit' criteria, or else it is judicial discretion filling a gap, not the application of pre-existing law.
modelAnswer.application: On Dworkin's framework, the employee's deliberate fraud closely mirrors Elmer Palmer's deliberate wrongdoing — serious, intentional misconduct directly connected to the benefit claimed — giving the 'no profit from wrong' principle real weight against the literal entitlement. A Hartian could accept the same outcome but describe it differently: either as an inclusive rule of recognition incorporating fit-based criteria, or as legitimate judicial discretion reasonably extending the scheme's rules to avoid an absurd result, rather than as the discovery of a principle that was silently part of the law all along.
modelAnswer.conclusion: A court could plausibly deny the pension on Riggs-style reasoning, but whether that shows Dworkin is right that this was binding law all along, or merely that a Hartian's rule of recognition (or judicial discretion) can reach the same result by a different route, remains exactly the unresolved dispute this lesson describes.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating Riggs v Palmer as having settled the Hart–Dworkin debate, or treating a principle that loses a weighing contest as if it had been invalidated like a repealed rule. Both mistakes come from importing the all-or-nothing logic of rules into a category — principles — that Dworkin deliberately defines to work differently.
